title: Comparing Agentic AI Products with Evidence
summary: After completing this intermediate module, learners can design and apply a provider-neutral comparison of agentic AI products using shared tasks, risk-based criteria, and documented evidence. They can distinguish product claims from observed test results and explain a defensible selection.
objectives: Define a common use case and success criteria for comparing agentic AI products.
Evaluate candidates using task performance, action control, human oversight, traceability, robustness, and resource-use criteria.
Separate documented product claims from results observed during testing.
Apply minimum acceptance gates before calculating an overall comparison result.
Explain a product selection by connecting evidence to the intended use and its risks.

sections.title: Currency correction
paragraphs: The previously cited source, content/modules/agentic-ai-literacy/agentic-product-comparison.json, was an unregistered local publisher path and had never been verified. It was removed and replaced with the official risk-management source listed at the end of this module.

This source change affects the evidentiary basis for the comparison method. The updated method connects evaluation to intended context, measurement, risk treatment, and governance. Any product-specific conclusion attributed only to the previous source is UNKNOWN and is omitted rather than repeated. No named product, provider ranking, version-specific conclusion, or configuration advice is introduced by this correction.
sections.callout: A source path inside a content repository is not independent evidence for the claims made by that same content.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can describe an AI task, identify an expected result, and write a basic pass-or-fail test. It does not assume knowledge of any named provider or product.

For this module, an agentic product is evaluated as a system that can pursue a goal through multiple steps and actions rather than producing only one isolated response. The comparison therefore examines both the final result and how actions are selected, constrained, recorded, and reviewed.

The official risk-management source organizes AI risk work around governing, mapping, measuring, and managing. A product comparison can follow the same logic: establish responsibilities, describe the intended context, gather measurements, and decide how identified risks will be handled.

sections.title: Define a common test
paragraphs: Begin with one intended use rather than a broad question about which candidate is best. Describe the user, goal, permitted inputs, permitted actions, prohibited actions, expected output, review process, and consequences of failure. A candidate that fits one use may not fit another.
Give every candidate equivalent tasks, information, permissions, time limits, and success criteria. If conditions differ, record the difference and do not treat the results as a direct comparison.

Create several representative cases, including an ordinary case, an ambiguous case, and a case in which the system should stop or request human review. Define the expected behavior before running the tests. This reduces the temptation to change the standard after seeing a preferred result.

sections.title: Use agentic comparison criteria
paragraphs: Task performance asks whether the candidate reaches the defined goal and whether its result satisfies the prewritten success criteria. Record both successful and unsuccessful cases rather than reporting only a favorable example.

Action control asks whether the candidate stays within permitted actions, respects prohibited actions, and pauses when required information or authority is missing. Human oversight asks whether a reviewer can interrupt, approve, reject, or correct consequential actions at the required points.

Traceability asks whether the available record lets a reviewer reconstruct important inputs, actions, outputs, approvals, and failures. Robustness asks whether performance remains acceptable when instructions are incomplete, inputs vary, or an action fails.

Resource use asks what the comparison consumes under the same test conditions. Record only units that can be observed consistently across candidates. Do not invent missing cost, time, or usage figures, and do not combine unlike units as if they were equivalent.

sections.title: Separate evidence and apply gates
paragraphs: Maintain separate records for documented claims and observed results. A documented claim reports what a source says the candidate can do. An observed result reports what happened in the defined test. A claim is not automatically a test result, and one successful run does not establish reliable performance.

Record each test case, expected behavior, observed behavior, pass-or-fail result, evidence location, and reviewer note. When evidence is missing or cannot be compared fairly, mark that criterion UNKNOWN and omit it from any asserted conclusion.

Set acceptance gates before assigning preferences. A gate is a condition that must be satisfied regardless of strengths elsewhere. For example, if the intended use requires human approval before a consequential action, a candidate that cannot satisfy that requirement fails the gate. A high result on another criterion must not cancel the failure.

After applying gates, compare the remaining candidates using criteria tied to the intended use. Explain the selection in terms of the evidence, limitations, and unresolved unknowns. Avoid claiming that the selected candidate is universally best.

sections.title: Follow a repeatable workflow
paragraphs: First, map the intended use, affected people, permissions, failure consequences, and oversight needs. Second, define measurable criteria and mandatory gates. Third, run equivalent test cases and preserve the evidence. Fourth, review failures and unknowns before comparing acceptable candidates. Finally, document the selection, its scope, and the conditions that would require reevaluation.

This workflow gives you a capability you did not need before the module: you can now turn an informal product preference into a provider-neutral comparison whose conclusion can be traced to a defined use case, common tests, mandatory safeguards, and recorded evidence.

questions.prompt: What did the source correction affect?
choices: It established a ranking of named products.
It replaced an unverified local source path and updated the evidentiary basis of the comparison method.
It supplied product-specific configuration advice.
It proved that every candidate has the same capabilities.
questions.explanation: The correction replaced an unverified local source path with an official risk-management source. Product-specific conclusions unsupported by a verified source remain UNKNOWN and are omitted.

questions.prompt: Which action is required for a direct comparison between candidates?
choices: Give each candidate equivalent tasks, information, permissions, time limits, and success criteria.
Change the success criteria after reviewing the first result.
Use only the most favorable example from each candidate.
Allow each candidate to perform different tasks without recording the differences.
questions.explanation: Equivalent conditions make the results comparable. Any unavoidable difference must be recorded and limits the strength of the comparison.

questions.prompt: Why should documented claims and observed results be recorded separately?
choices: Because a documented claim is automatically stronger than a test result.
Because observed results do not require a defined test.
Because a statement about a capability is not the same as evidence of what occurred in the comparison test.
Because only documented claims may be used in a comparison.
questions.explanation: A documented claim states what a source says, while an observed result records what happened under defined test conditions.

questions.prompt: A use case requires human approval before a consequential action, but a candidate cannot provide that approval point. What should the evaluator do?
choices: Ignore the requirement if the candidate performs well on another criterion.
Change the requirement after testing.
Treat the missing approval point as a failed mandatory gate.
Mark every other candidate as failed.
questions.explanation: A mandatory gate must be satisfied regardless of strengths elsewhere. Performance on another criterion cannot cancel the missing required safeguard.

questions.prompt: How should the evaluator handle a criterion for which comparable evidence is missing?
choices: Estimate a favorable result.
Mark it UNKNOWN and omit it from asserted conclusions.
Copy the result from another criterion.
Assume all candidates perform equally.
questions.explanation: The module directs evaluators to mark missing or incomparable evidence as UNKNOWN rather than inventing a result.
